prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and of its active form, which made possible incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: one prize part, B044, to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. Round 1 showed that all six of us reach it, but I do not count that as evidence. The case is scientific. Proglucagon processing, the active truncated GLP-1 peptide, glucose-dependent insulin secretion, effects on appetite and gastric emptying in humans, and receptor biology form a complete discovery chain, and large independent randomized trials have confirmed benefit in diabetes, obesity, and cardiovascular and renal outcomes. The field is mature, the interpretation is stable, and no member argued the case is premature. A single-part prize keeps the citation on the physiological discovery. The three-person budget is fully used here, and I have not seen a second achievement that can be configured fairly within the remaining budget, so I do not propose a second part.
statement.case_against: Attribution remains the weak point and I cannot close it from the ballot record. The supplied names are not the full history: Habener is absent, Mojsov's priority is publicly contested, and the cap excludes Knudsen, whose long-acting analogue design turned the physiology into a therapy. Excluding her has a real cost, and a discovery-framed citation can read as ignoring the step that reached patients. I accept that cost deliberately because the prize rewards the discovery of the physiological principle and the active peptide, and because adding a name would mean dropping one of three people whose separable discovery steps are each documented. The record should say that the exclusion reflects the cap and the discovery framing, not a view that her work was minor.

responses.point: Perlmann keeps the trio on discovery grounds, defends Mojsov's distinct peptide-identification step despite the public dispute, and argues that CAR-T cannot be configured fairly without Eshhar.
responses.response: I agree that public dispute over credit is a reason to read the primary record, not to drop Mojsov, and the peptide-identification step is distinct from Holst's physiology and Drucker's biology. On B018 I take your point that I understated the gap. With Eshhar outside the credited names, any trio we can propose is partial, and Rosenberg's adoptive cell therapy fits a CAR-specific citation only in part. I therefore still treat B018 as an alternative, not as a second part. Where I part from you slightly is on Knudsen: the cost of leaving her out is larger than your wording suggests, and I would want it stated openly.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius would keep the supplied trio, wants the record to state that the credited list is incomplete, and says a two-part prize would need a different three-person budget that B044 does not leave.
responses.response: We agree. I will vote only on supplied names and want the record to say the list is incomplete, including Habener's absence, rather than imply attribution is settled. I also accept your arithmetic. A second part would have to come from the same three-person budget, so a two-part prize means cutting one of the three GLP-1 names, which the attribution does not support. That, more than any weakness in B012 or B018, is why I do not propose a second part. One correction: some members attribute to me a Sabatini concern. My round 1 file rests nothing on anyone's later professional history, and I would decide B013 only on documented scientific contribution.

responses.point: El-Manira says optogenetics is a method, that the prize-worthy step is channelrhodopsin function (Nagel, Hegemann, Bamberg), and that a Deisseroth-Hegemann-Nagel trio credits application at the expense of Bamberg, Boyden and Miesenboeck; he would rank CAR-T above it.
responses.response: I have reconsidered B001 in light of this. We agree that a Deisseroth, Hegemann and Nagel trio leaves out three credible contributors. Your split is useful, because channelrhodopsin function and neuronal implementation are separable and each could be a part of its own. But the cap makes that unworkable beside B044: two parts would need at least four names and omit people with defensible claims. I still hold method-driven discoveries as eligible, and optogenetics is of enormous reach, but I now place it below B018 for this year. I keep it in my alternatives only because the chair's second alternative slot is open, and because it may be overdue. I would not let it displace B044.

responses.point: Linnarsson says the Walter and Mori pair (B012) is the cleanest attribution and a textbook-mature concept, and says the UPR could be a second part if the committee wants two achievements.
responses.response: I agree B012 has the cleanest attribution on the shortlist. My remaining concern is balance. Its impact is mainly conceptual, with limited clinical translation after about three decades, and B044 combines comparable originality with verified outcomes at population scale. I said in round 1 that I would not object to B012 as a second part in some year, and I hold that, but a second part this year would require one of the three GLP-1 names to go. It is a fair candidate for a later year, not a reason to dilute B044's citation now.

uncertainties: How the credit for the active GLP-1 peptide should be weighed between Mojsov, Habener and Holst; I cannot verify priority from the ballot evidence and Habener is not a credited ballot name.
Whether the citation should mention the therapy so that excluding Knudsen is not read as a judgment on her work; I lean toward naming incretin-based treatment while crediting only the discovery.
Whether B018 can be configured fairly given Eshhar's absence and Rosenberg's partial fit, which is why it is an alternative only.
Whether optogenetics is eligible as a discovery and which separable achievement (channelrhodopsin function or neuronal application) a future prize would recognize.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. No conflict with any shortlisted candidate applies. My Rockefeller postdoc with Paul Greengard and my roughly twenty co-authored works with Thomas Perlmann (dopamine neurons, Nurr1, autophagy) concern no shortlisted ballot, and I know of no relationship with any credited name. Shared institution or topic is not treated as a personal tie. As chair I count only positions stated explicitly in the written record, and I do not seek recusal.
